title: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 3.5 Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion
intro: After this lesson you can define the parameter, state the null and alternative hypotheses, check the conditions with the null proportion, and name a one-sample $z$ test for a population proportion.

moments.title: Hypothesis test
moments.text: A procedure that uses sample data to decide about a claim for a population parameter. Here, a one-sample $z$ test for a proportion.

moments.title: Two forms of inference
moments.text: A confidence interval estimates the parameter. A test checks a claim about it.

moments.title: Restaurant takeout
moments.text: The chain claims more than 60% order takeout. In a sample of 250, 170 did, so $\hat p=0.68$.

moments.title: Two reasons $\hat p$ can differ
moments.text: Samples vary, or the truth really is different. The test helps decide between them.

moments.title: Light bulbs
moments.text: A maker claims fewer than 8% are defective. In a sample of 650, 42 were, so $\hat p\approx0.065$.

moments.title: Remote learning
moments.text: A board thinks the proportion of parents who support it differs from 50%. In 300 parents, 141 do.

moments.title: Putting a proportion on trial
moments.text: Assume the null value is true, then ask whether the sample gives convincing evidence against it.

moments.title: PHANTOM
moments.text: Parameter, Hypotheses, Assumptions, Name, Test statistic, Obtain the p-value, Make a conclusion. This lesson covers the first four.

moments.title: Parameter and name in one sentence
moments.text: "A one-sample $z$ test for $p$, the proportion of all ... who ..."

moments.title: Check the conditions
moments.text: Random sample, $n$ at most 10% of the population, and at least 10 expected successes and failures.

moments.title: Use $p_0$ for large counts, not $\hat p$
moments.text: Check $np_0\ge10$ and $n(1-p_0)\ge10$ with the null proportion.

moments.title: Null and alternative hypotheses
moments.text: $H_0$ is the status quo. $H_a$ is the claim the test looks for evidence of.

moments.title: Always $p$, never $\hat p$
moments.text: Hypotheses are about the population parameter.

moments.title: Same number, equal sign in the null
moments.text: $H_0$ always uses $=$, and both hypotheses use the same value.

moments.title: One-sided and two-sided tests
moments.text: $>$ is an upper test, $<$ is a lower test, and $\ne$ is a two-sided test.

moments.title: Tails of the null distribution
moments.text: Only the tail in the direction of $H_a$ matters. A two-sided test uses both tails.

moments.title: The setup does not use the sample
moments.text: Parameter, hypotheses, conditions and name all come from the claim, not from $\hat p$.

moments.title: Dog park
moments.text: The council builds the park only with evidence that more than 75% want it. Sample: 361 of 465.

moments.title: Pick the correct hypotheses
moments.text: The claim is the alternative, the null uses $=$, and neither uses $\hat p$.

cards.name: Upper test
cards.text: The claim says more than, greater than, or higher than $p_0$.

cards.name: Lower test
cards.text: The claim says fewer than, less than, or lower than $p_0$.

cards.name: Two-sided test
cards.text: The claim says different from, changed from, or not equal to $p_0$.

cells: More than 60% of customers order takeout
Fewer than 8% of bulbs are defective
The share of parents who support remote learning differs from 50%

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video treats "at least 35%" as "more than 35%" in its multiple-choice example. A claim of "at least" or "at most" includes the boundary, so read the problem for a strict word such as more than, fewer than or different from before choosing $H_a$. On the exam, $H_0$ is still written with an equals sign.

sections.title: Set up a test with PHANTOM
sections.intro: The first four PHANTOM steps set up the test. None of them uses the sample proportion. The last three steps (test statistic, p-value, conclusion) come in topics 3.6 and 3.7.
steps: Parameter: define $p$ with the population and the response variable.
Hypotheses: $H_0: p=p_0$ and $H_a$ with $<$, $>$ or $\ne$, using the same number.
Assumptions: random sample, $n$ at most 10% of the population, and $np_0\ge10$, $n(1-p_0)\ge10$.
Name the test: one-sample $z$ test for a population proportion. Steps 1 and 4 fit in one sentence.

parts.label: Parameter and name
parts.tex: $p=$ proportion of all Oakville residents who favor the dog park

parts.label: Random and 10%
parts.text: Assume the city has more than 4,650 residents when the size is not given.

parts.label: Hypotheses
parts.text: The council wants evidence of more than 75%.

sections.line: $\text{Setup uses }p_0\text{ and the claim, never }\hat p$

sections.title: Which tail counts?
sections.intro: Switch between $H_a: p<p_0$, $H_a: p>p_0$ and $H_a: p\ne p_0$ and watch which tail of the null distribution is shaded. The curve is centered at $p_0$ and is built assuming $H_0$ is true. You will use the $z$ and p-value readouts in topics 3.6 and 3.7; for now, look only at the tails.

stories.rest: A restaurant chain claims more than 60% of customers order takeout. In a random sample of 250 customers, 170 ordered takeout. $H_a: p>0.60$.
stories.bulb: A company claims fewer than 8% of its light bulbs are defective. In a random sample of 650 bulbs, 42 were defective. $H_a: p<0.08$.
stories.remote: A school board believes the share of parents who support remote learning is different from 50%. In a random sample of 300 parents, 141 support it. $H_a: p\ne0.50$.
stories.dog: A city will build a dog park only if more than 75% of residents want it. In a random sample of 465 residents, 361 want it. $H_a: p>0.75$.

sections.title: Write it so it earns credit

traps.title: Putting $\hat p$ in the hypotheses
traps.better: $H_0: p=0.60$ and $H_a: p>0.60$, where $p$ is the proportion of all customers who order takeout.

traps.title: Checking large counts with the sample proportion
Defining the parameter
traps.weak: $p$ is the proportion who order takeout.
traps.better: $p$ is the proportion of all customers of the restaurant chain who order takeout rather than dine in.

traps.title: Naming the test
traps.better: A one-sample $z$ test for a population proportion.

traps.title: Writing the null with an inequality or a different number
traps.better: $H_0: p=0.35$ and $H_a: p>0.35$. The equals sign is always in $H_0$, and both hypotheses use the same number.

questions.stem: A coach claims that more than 40% of the players in a large league are left-handed. In a random sample of 120 players, 54 are left-handed. Which are the correct hypotheses?
why: The claim is the alternative, the null uses $=$, and both use the same value and the parameter $p$.
Hypotheses are about the population parameter, not the sample proportion.
The sample proportion 54/120 = 0.45 does not appear in the hypotheses.
The claim belongs in $H_a$, and the null has the equals sign.

questions.stem: A test of $H_0: p=0.30$ is based on a random sample of 120 players, 45 of whom are successes. Which pair of calculations checks the large counts condition?
why: These use the sample proportion 0.375, which is not used in a test.
Use the null value: $np_0=36$ and $n(1-p_0)=84$, both at least 10.
The sample count is not multiplied by $p_0$.
The second count must use $1-p_0$, and neither uses $\hat p$.

questions.stem: A test has alternative hypothesis $H_a: p\ne0.50$. What kind of test is this?
why: The $\ne$ symbol means evidence in either direction counts, so both tails are used.
A paired test compares two measurements on the same subjects.

questions.stem: Which statement about the setup of a one-sample $z$ test for $p$ is correct?
opts: The standard deviation of the null distribution is found from $\hat p$
The conditions are checked with the sample proportion
The hypotheses and the conditions use $p_0$ and not $\hat p$
The alternative hypothesis uses the sample proportion
why: The null distribution is built assuming $H_0$ is true, so it uses $p_0$.
Large counts use the null proportion in a test.
The setup comes from the claim, not from the sample.
The alternative is about $p$, the population parameter.

sections.title: Write a full response
sections.prompt: A battery manufacturer claims that 90% of its batteries last more than 10 hours. A consumer group suspects the true percentage is lower. The group tests a random sample of 180 batteries from a shipment of 5,000, and 154 last more than 10 hours.
parts: (a) Name the procedure and define the parameter.
(c) Check the conditions for the procedure.
(d) Explain why the sample proportion $154/180$ is not used in parts (b) and (c).
sample: (a) A one-sample $z$ test for a population proportion. $p$ is the proportion of all batteries in the shipment that last more than 10 hours.
(c) Random: the 180 batteries were a random sample. 10%: 180 is less than 10% of 5,000, which is 500. Large counts: $180(0.90)=162\ge10$ and $180(0.10)=18\ge10$.

(d) The test begins by assuming $H_0$ is true, so the hypotheses and the conditions use the null value 0.90. The sample proportion 0.856 is the evidence that will be compared with 0.90 in the test statistic.
checklist: (a) One-sample $z$ test for a population proportion, with the parameter defined in context
(b) $H_0: p=0.90$ and $H_a: p<0.90$ with $p$, not $\hat p$
(d) Says the setup uses the null value and the sample proportion is evidence used later
